source.title: The Spotlight Resonance Method: Resolving the Alignment of Embedded Activations

record.tranche_reason: The study uses its own Spotlight-Resonance Method to measure whether learned activations align with individual privileged basis directions. This is a different measurement from the original superposition work and does not test superposition itself.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SRM measurements of learned activation distributions and signed-SRM measurements for hand-picked directions. Hyperparameters such as the spotlight threshold are not treated as outcomes. Claims cited from other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study measures whether autoencoder latent activations cluster around the basis privileged by a custom activation function, using SRM. This is basis alignment, a construct borrowed from Toy Models' 'privileged basis'. It does not measure features outnumbering dimensions, interference, polysemanticity, SAE features, or 1-D versus multi-dimensional features. Superposition and capacity come up only as speculation. Axis alignment says nothing about feature dimensionality, so the record's link to V6 is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add that the author claims a direct causal link: activation-function functional forms induce the privileged basis that representations align to. The author also concludes that prior standard-basis (neuron) alignment comes from elementwise activations, not from anything innate.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces SRM, a rotation-and-spotlight measurement of activation alignment; it does not report a reproduction of the original study's method. The original method details needed for a more specific comparison are not stated here.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with the privileged basis and its completeness; the text also reports that some settings require a lower epsilon to reveal signal.

fits_no_version.finding: Trained autoencoder latents align or anti-align with whatever basis the activation function privileges. They show no signal on standard or random bases when a non-standard basis is privileged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-function symmetry breaking determines which basis representations align with. Neuron-basis alignment is not intrinsic to the standard basis.

fits_no_version.finding: Some hand-picked privileged directions in reconstruction autoencoders respond to human-interpretable concepts (sky/water, vehicles, eyes, digit shapes). The author calls this preliminary and subjective.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grandmother-like privileged-basis neurons can arise spontaneously in self-supervised fully connected autoencoders.

record.peer_reviewed: To appear at the ICLR 2025 Workshop on Representational Alignment (Re-Align)
record.problems: The paper describes the local-coding findings as preliminary and subjective, says that the results do not establish local coding across the full network, and notes that some interpretations and geometric effects need further investigation. The reported SRM results are presented mainly in plots rather than numerical tables; no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately described SRM outcomes bearing on V6 were left out. Broad statements about results across other tested networks are not entered as separate rows because the text does not identify those models or give separately attributable outcomes.

untested.parts: No sparse-feature toy model, no features exceeding dimensions, no sparsity transition or geometry.
Capacity is discussed only speculatively (anti-alignment gives 2^n capacity). No feature importance or capacity manipulation.
No comparison of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features. Alignment with basis directions does not bear on feature dimensionality.

record.verdict_notes: Toy Models is cited only for the term 'privileged basis'. Superposition is mentioned only as a possible explanation for amplitude variation. All results are figure-only, with no uncertainty estimates, and the setups are MNIST/CIFAR autoencoders with a custom generalised tanh.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test sparse features competing for more features than dimensions, their interference, or a sparsity-dependent transition and geometry.
Does not manipulate capacity or feature importance, or test whether important features get dedicated dimensions while others share.
Does not measure polysemantic neurons or test whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure.
Tests autoencoders on MNIST and CIFAR, not LLMs or SAE-recovered features.
Does not test SAE features for completeness, stability, or canonical status.

Measures alignment with one-dimensional privileged directions and reports examples of individual meaningful directions, but does not study superposition itself or compare one-dimensional with multidimensional features.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Trained autoencoders and selected privileged directions
reader_labels.reason: SRM and signed-SRM show learned activations aligned with privileged directions, including directions associated by the author with human-interpretable patterns (r1, r3, r6-r12, r14).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Across different privileged bases and model settings
reader_labels.reason: The standard and random basis controls lack a meaningful signal, simplex directions are anti-aligned, and another overcomplete setting is reported as diffuse and opposing the directions; the study does not test superposition or rule out multidimensional features (r4, r5, r13, r15).
